newsitem.title: GERMANY: Meister warns of danger in govts using derivatives.
newsitem.headline: Meister warns of danger in govts using derivatives.

text.p: Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister said on Tuesday that the state must take great care when using derivative instruments to manage its debt and warned governments against placing excessive faith in them.
Meister said that in theory the public sector can conduct derivative transactions to an unlimited extent and that any losses from such deals would directly burden the taxpayer.
"The use of such instruments must be carefully assessed from the point of view of risk and cost savings potential and an abuse must be ruled out," Meister said in the text of a speech.
He called for a uniform gauge which estimated the benefits and risks of derivatives deals done by public authorities.
Meister noted that while the German federal government conducted virtually no derivative deals, some states or Laender had recently been trying to reduce their debt costs through interest rate swaps.
German municipalities tended to use derivatives only as an exception, although some had conducted currency swaps, Meister said.
He said public authorities should be aware of their particular responsibility to the country and its citizens and should only use derivatives as hedging instruments, never for speculation.
"In practise it may in some cases not be so easy to distinguish clearly between hedging transactions and speculative transactions," he added.
He cited losses on swap transactions incurred by a number of British local authorities in the 1980s as an example of how dangerous speculative deals can be.

The Hammersmith and Fulham authority at the end of the 1980s conducted interest rate hedging deals with a nominal volume of about six billion British pounds while the authority's debt in this period only amounted to about 400 million pounds, Meister said.
"Such a use of -- predominantly -- interest rate swaps to a disproportionate extent proves that these instruments were mainly used for speculative purposes."
But even if derivative deals are limited to hedging, losses cannot be ruled out, Meister said.
